title: The talent was always Indian. September 8, 2026.
excerpt: From a Pentium architect who left India in the 1970s to venture partners writing checks from Silicon Valley today, September 8 traced one throughline: Indian talent has been building the world's technology for fifty years, and it's finally building back home too.
bodyHtml:
Some days in this project line up by coincidence. September 8 wasn't one of them - once the day's five stories were written, a single thread ran through nearly all of them: talent that leaves doesn't disappear. It compounds, somewhere else, and eventually starts flowing back.

The chip architect nobody in India learned about in school

Start with Vinod Dham. Born in Pune, trained as an electrical engineer in Delhi, Dham left for the United States in the 1970s and joined Intel - decades before India had anything resembling its own semiconductor industry. He became one of the lead architects behind the Pentium processor, the chip that powered the entire personal computer boom of the 1990s. Inside the industry, people still call him the "father of the Pentium chip." The architecture decisions his team made in that era are still echoing through how processors get built today.

Dham's story isn't a footnote in Indian history - it's a preview. Decades before India built its own chip-design ecosystem, Indian engineers were already shaping the hardware the entire world runs on. That's not a coincidence the country is only now catching up to; it's the same talent pool that global semiconductor firms are opening new design centers in India to tap into.

The venture money moving the other direction now

Fast forward to today, and the pattern has a second half. Some of the biggest checks written into Indian startups don't come from India at all - they come from Indian-origin investors sitting inside Silicon Valley's top venture firms. TiE, The Indus Entrepreneurs, now runs more than 60 chapters worldwide, almost entirely built by Indian-origin founders and investors mentoring the next generation. Partners of Indian origin now sit inside firms like Sequoia, Khosla Ventures and General Catalyst as actual decision-makers, not just employees - and many of them personally angel-invest in Indian startups on the side, often writing the earliest checks before an Indian VC ever sees the deal.

Put next to Dham's story, this isn't really a new trend. It's the same one, one generation later: Indian engineering judgment, tested in the world's toughest markets, eventually finding its way back to India - first as talent, now increasingly as capital too.

The sector actually moving fast enough to notice

If you want a live example of where that capital and talent could keep landing, electric vehicles are it. India's EV sales just crossed 12% of every new vehicle sold - a record, and a fast one. EV retail sales hit over 306,000 units in a single month, up 41 times from just 50,000 units sold back in 2016. Two-wheelers are leading the shift, not cars: over half of every EV sold today is a scooter or a bike. Nearly 400 EV startups are now building everything from charging networks to batteries. The government's target is 30% penetration by 2030 - the gap is closing, but cars and trucks are still lagging well behind two-wheelers.

It's not a finished transition. But it's a curve bending faster every year, and it's exactly the kind of sector where returning capital and returning engineers tend to land first.

A regional voice that became a national one, decades before social media could do it for him

Zoom out from technology and money for a moment, because September 8 is also Bhupen Hazarika's birthday. Born in Sadiya, Assam in 1926, Hazarika cut his first record at age 10, earned a PhD in mass communication from Columbia University, and came home to build a career as a singer, songwriter, filmmaker and public intellectual. He wrote mostly in Assamese - but his songs about humanity and universal brotherhood got translated and sung across the entire country for decades, carrying a regional voice into a genuinely national one, long before any platform existed to do that work automatically. He received the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 2019.

It's a reminder that the growth story sitting underneath everything else in this newsletter isn't only measured in chip architectures or venture rounds - it's also built by people working in every language and region, not just the ones that dominate headlines today.

The unglamorous tools nobody puts in a headline

And then there's the smallest story of the day, which might be the most honest one: a scooter that gets someone to their first job interview does more for India's growth story than most headlines give it credit for. Progress isn't only the big, visible bets - the chip architectures, the venture rounds, the record EV sales. It's also the small, unglamorous tools that let ordinary people show up and try. A 20-year story toward 2047 is built from a lot of those, not just the ones that make the news.

Five stories, one day. None of them are the whole picture on their own - the picture is what they add up to.

Born on September 8th, the voice that carried Assam to the rest of India.
The scooter that got someone to their first job interview is doing more for India's growth story than most headlines give it credit for.
He designed the microprocessor architecture that still shapes chips inside billions of devices today.
Some of the biggest checks written into Indian startups don't come from India. They come from Indian-origin investors sitting inside Silicon Valley's top venture firms.
